To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we developed a platform to transfer prokaryotic sensors to mammalian cells and used the platform to create a set of new sensors that can sense diverse small molecules and respond to the signals with a range of dynamic range and threshold.
the TetR family of transcriptional regulators can be used to construct synthetic sensors and circuits in mammalian cells.
we present a platform that systematically enables the transfer of TetR-family repressors and activators from prokaryotes to mammalian cells and use them to build a suite of new sensors and circuits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of genetic circuits in mammalian cells.
the development of new genetic tools for mammalian cells.
the development of new tools for synthetic biology, and in particular the construction of mammalian genetic circuits and their application to the design of living therapeutics.

this is a very interesting and useful study.
the work presented here introduces a general strategy to systematically transfer prokaryotic sensors and circuits to mammalian cells.
this work introduces a generic and modular approach to develop genetic sensors and circuits in mammalian cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

it provides a generalizable platform to transfer prokaryotic regulators to mammalian systems, demonstrating the ability to construct 15 new regulators, 3 NOT gates, 1 fuzzy AND gate, and 2 small molecule sensing systems.
we present a new approach that allows for the transfer of prokaryotic regulators into mammalian cells.
the TetR family is a rich source of genetic regulators that can be used to build synthetic sensors and circuits in mammalian cells.

the TetR family of transcription factors are highly modular and their activity can be tuned by modifying their DNA-binding affinity.
it is possible to transfer the sensing and regulation mechanisms of bacterial regulators to mammalian systems.
